# Cross-compiling and deploying binaries

A binary built on your laptop does not automatically run on another machine. The executable file
format differs between operating systems, and so do the processor instructions. Nim can aim its
output at another system, but not with a single magic switch: the result is only as good as the C
toolchain available on the machine doing the build.

::: {.callout-note}
## What you will be able to do

After this chapter you can pick a target with `--os` and `--cpu`, set features from the command line
with `-d:` and `{.strdefine.}`, tell `-d:release`, `--opt:speed`, and `-d:danger` apart, build a
static binary, and recognize when cross-compiling must fail because the toolchain is missing.
:::

## Choosing a target: `--os` and `--cpu`

Two switches decide the destination. `--os` picks the operating system and `--cpu` picks the
processor family. Common values: `linux`, `windows`, `macosx` for systems, and `amd64`, `arm64`,
`i386`, `arm` for processors.

The safest way to inspect the target is to ask the compiler. `defined` and `when` are answered before
the program runs, while `hostOS` and `hostCPU` hold the same names for the running program to read.
Both come from `system`, so no import is needed.

```{.nim}
# The compiler resolves this `when` before the program runs.
const isWindows =
  when defined(windows): true
  else: false

const isUnixLike =
  when defined(linux) or defined(macosx) or defined(freebsd) or defined(openbsd): true
  else: false

const isLinux =
  when defined(linux): true
  else: false

echo "isWindows: ", isWindows
echo "isUnixLike: ", isUnixLike
echo "hostOS agrees with defined(linux): ", (hostOS == "linux") == isLinux
echo "hostCPU is set: ", hostCPU.len > 0
```

```{.txt}
isWindows: false
isUnixLike: true
hostOS agrees with defined(linux): true
hostCPU is set: true
```

This example deliberately does not print the raw `hostOS` and `hostCPU` values. Those differ between
the development machine and the checking machine, so the output block would never match. What is
printed are comparisons that are identical on every unix-like machine: whether the `when` branch
agrees with `hostOS`, and whether `hostCPU` is set.

## Turning features on from the command line

Besides `--os` and `--cpu` there is `-d:name` for defining a symbol. The symbol is read by `when`, so
a build choice never requires a code change.

```{.nim}
# `-d:symbol` sets a compile-time flag that `when` can see.
when defined(release):
  const buildKind = "release"
else:
  const buildKind = "debug"

# `{.strdefine.}` and `{.intdefine.}` read their value from `-d:name=value`.
const targetName {.strdefine.} = "host"
const workers {.intdefine.} = 1

echo "build kind: ", buildKind
echo "target name: ", targetName
echo "workers: ", workers
```

```{.txt}
build kind: debug
target name: host
workers: 1
```

Without extra switches the output is as above: default build, default name, one worker. Run with
`nim c -r -d:release -d:targetName=server -d:workers=4`, and the first line becomes `release` while
the next two follow the values you gave.

`{.strdefine.}` and `{.intdefine.}` give a default value that can still be overridden from outside.
This is the pattern many programs use: one binary, several configurations, without touching the code.

## `-d:release`, `--opt:speed`, and `-d:danger`

The same code, different results. The example files in this book's repository keep their compile
switches in a `.mode` file, so the automated check compiles them the same way as written here.

```{.nim}
when defined(release):
  echo "build kind: release"
else:
  echo "build kind: debug"

when defined(danger):
  echo "danger define is set"
else:
  echo "danger define is not set"
```

```{.txt}
build kind: release
danger define is not set
```

The example above is run with `nim c -r -d:release`. `-d:release` turns optimization on and disables
stack traces; runtime checks stay in place. `--opt:speed` only turns optimization on, leaving
everything else alone. `-d:danger` goes further: it turns off all runtime checks.

```{.nim}
when defined(danger):
  echo "danger define is set"
else:
  echo "danger define is not set"

when defined(release):
  echo "release is implied by danger"
else:
  echo "release is not set"
```

```{.txt}
danger define is set
release is implied by danger
```

That output comes from `nim c -r -d:danger`, and two things are visible at once. `danger` is indeed
set, and it brings `release` along. The consequence is real: an array index past its bounds is no
longer reported as a defect, it silently reads memory outside its data. Keep `-d:danger` for binaries
already proven correct, not for the stage where you are still writing code.

## Static binaries

A binary compiled on one distribution sometimes refuses to run on another because the C library
version differs. The linker can be asked to fold every library into the binary:

```bash
nim c -d:release --passL:-static --out:app app.nim
```

The result is a static binary: it does not look for C libraries at run time, so it is safer to move
around. This switch is for Linux targets. The macOS linker does not know it, and on Nim 2.2.12 the
attempt stops with `ld: library 'crt0.o' not found`.

`--passL` forwards options to the linker and `--passC` forwards options to the C compiler. Both are
the bridge for cases Nim has no switch of its own for:

```bash
nim c --passC:-DLOG_LEVEL=2 --passL:-lm --out:app app.nim
```

Use both sparingly. An option the C compiler does not understand breaks the build, and that message
comes from the C compiler, not from Nim.

## Deliberate error: `when` needs a compile-time value

`when` is not `if`. Its branch is chosen during compilation, so the condition has to be computable
right then.

```{.nim}
import std/os

let requested = paramStr(0)

# `when` needs a value that is known before the program runs.
when requested.len > 0:
  echo "the program has a name"
```

```{.txt}
main.nim(6, 6) Error: cannot evaluate at compile time: requested
```

The message points at line 6, column 6, right at the start of the name `requested`, then explains
why: the value is only known while the program runs. `paramStr(0)` reads an argument from the
operating system, and that happens after the binary starts. The fix is to replace `when` with `if`,
or to move the condition into a `const` that can be computed during compilation.

## The limit: a C toolchain for the target

`--os` and `--cpu` only tell Nim where you want to go. What actually shapes the binary is the C
compiler, and it has to be available for that target.

```bash
# Needs a MinGW toolchain; without one the C compiler stops at windows.h.
nim c -d:mingw --os:windows --cpu:amd64 --out:app.exe app.nim
```

Without that toolchain the build stops in the C compiler with
`fatal error: 'windows.h' file not found`. On Linux, the MinGW packages provide
`x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc`, and Nim already ships the mapping for it in `config/nim.cfg` under
`@if unix and mingw`.

A subtler behaviour: changing `--os` alone does not always fail. On macOS, `--os:linux --cpu:amd64`
runs to completion and leaves a Mach-O file behind, not an ELF one. Nim believes it built a Linux
binary, while the C compiler kept producing a host binary. Such a file is useless; the mistake only
shows up much later, when it is started on the destination machine.

## Commands per target

A few commands that come up often, with their notes:

```bash
# Native release build for the machine doing the compiling.
nim c -d:release --out:app app.nim
```

```bash
# Linux target with a static C runtime, then copy the binary to the server.
nim c -d:release --passL:-static --out:app app.nim
scp ./app server:/srv/app/app
ssh server 'chmod +x /srv/app/app && /srv/app/app --version'
```

A project that uses nimble can pass the same switches through `nimble build`, because extra arguments
are forwarded to the Nim compiler:

```bash
nimble build --os:windows --cpu:amd64 -d:release
```

## Exercises

1. Name the `--os` and `--cpu` values for the machine you write code on, then compare them with the
   output of the first example.
2. Without running it, predict the output if the second example is compiled with
   `-d:release -d:workers=8`.
3. Write a program that prints `"windows target"` or `"unix target"` using `when defined`, then say
   what happens to the branch that is not chosen.
4. The code below fails to compile. Fix it, then explain the message: `let mode = paramStr(1)`
   followed by `when mode == "--debug": echo "debug"`.
5. Name two things that must be present before cross-compiling to Windows really produces a binary,
   and say what happens when one of them is missing.

Answers are in [Appendix A](../appendix/answers.qmd).

## Summary

- `--os` and `--cpu` pick the target; `when defined(...)`, `hostOS`, and `hostCPU` read it from
  inside the code.
- `-d:name` sets a compile-time symbol; `{.strdefine.}` and `{.intdefine.}` take its value.
- `-d:release` turns optimization on, `--opt:speed` handles optimization alone, and `-d:danger` turns
  off every check.
- `--passC` and `--passL` forward options to the C compiler and the linker; `--passL:-static` builds a
  static binary on Linux.
- Cross-compiling needs a C toolchain for the target. Without one, the build stops or produces a host
  binary that is useless.
